text: Why does spicy food feel hot?

steps.title: Capsaicin meets a nerve
steps.say: Chilli contains capsaicin. In your mouth it slips through the lining and sticks to receptors on the tips of tiny pain-and-heat nerves.

composed.caption: Capsaicin reaching a heat-sensing nerve in the tongue
composed.basis: Textbook TRPV1 physiology (Caterina et al., 1997, Nature)

steps.title: A lock meant for heat
steps.say: That receptor, called TRPV1, normally opens only when tissue gets hotter than about 43 °C. Capsaicin pries it open at normal temperature, so the nerve fires exactly as if burned.

composed.caption: The heat receptor fires without real heat
composed.basis: Textbook TRPV1 physiology (Caterina et al., 1997, Nature)

steps.title: The brain reads it as fire
steps.say: The signal arrives on the same line real burns use, and your brain can't tell the difference. So it labels it 'hot', though nothing in your mouth has warmed at all.

composed.caption: The burn signal reaches the brain
composed.basis: Standard textbook account of pain and temperature pathways

steps.title: The body tries to cool down
steps.say: Believing you're overheating, the brain widens skin vessels and turns on sweat, tears and a runny nose. That's why your face flushes and your forehead beads.

steps.title: It follows the food down
steps.say: The stomach and gut carry the same receptors, so a very hot meal can burn again on the way down and on the way out.

composed.caption: Capsaicin on the stomach lining's nerves
composed.basis: TRPV1 is expressed along the gut (Holzer, Pharmacological Reviews 2008)

steps.title: Why it fades; why milk helps
steps.say: Firing nerves tire and go quiet for a while, which is why regular chilli eaters feel less. Capsaicin dissolves in fat, so milk washes it away better than water or beer.

composed.caption: Tired nerve, capsaicin washed off
composed.basis: Capsaicin desensitisation and fat solubility, standard pharmacology

lines.text: Chilli's capsaicin switches on the nerve sensor that normally fires only for real heat.
Your brain can't tell the difference, so it reads a burn and starts cooling you down.
You may sweat and flush, though your temperature stays the same. Milk washes capsaicin off best.
